title: A hymn in Gujri
hook: a crane flies far from her chicks; who feeds them?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Gujri, music for devotion with no audience, and your line was quiet devotion.

A crane lifts off from a marsh and flies a long way, leaving her chicks behind in the reeds. Who feeds them while she's gone? Who teaches them anything? That question isn't from a nature program. It's from a hymn of Guru Arjan in Raga Gujri, one that a Sikh praying the evening Rehras says aloud. A small surprise: yesterday's raga belongs to the morning, yet some of its hymns are carried into the evening prayer.
screen: `A CRANE FLIES FAR.` → `WHO FEEDS THE CHICKS?` → `A GUJRI HYMN AT EVENING.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens by talking to the mind, in plain English: why, mind, do you keep scheming and straining, when the Lord himself is already busy with your care? Then the pictures come. In rocks and stones the Creator places living things, and sets their food in front of them. Then the crane. She flies far away, her chicks are left behind, and no one is there to feed them or teach them to peck. Think about it in your mind, the hymn says. Who looks after them? Guru Arjan isn't telling anyone to stop working; Sikh teaching prizes honest labor. The target is the anxious part of the mind that plans every outcome as if everything rested on it, still running the numbers at two in the morning. Against that, the hymn sets a slower trust: you do your part, and the care was there before you started. The same raga holds a very different voice. Bhagat Trilochan, one of the saints whose words the Gurus gathered into the Granth, asks a sharper question in Gujri: at the very end, what fills the mind? Thoughts of wealth, of wife and sons, of a fine mansion, each one shapes what comes next, he says, and only the one who remembers the Lord goes free. Two voices, one raga. One soothes an anxious mind; one wakes a distracted one. Both bring it back to the same place: steady, unshowy devotion, pointed at what matters.
screen: `WHY SCHEME AND STRAIN, MIND?` · `FOOD SET OUT IN THE ROCKS.` · `WHO FEEDS THE CRANE'S CHICKS?` · `TRILOCHAN: WHAT FILLS THE MIND AT THE END?` · then, large: `DEVOTION IN GUJRI.`

segments.voice: Breathe out longer than you breathe in, find the plan your mind keeps rehearsing today, the email, the bill, the conversation, and picture setting it on the floor beside you; it'll still be there after. For now, picture the crane's chicks in the reeds, fed by no effort of their own. If you pray, say Waheguru and let the worry rest there; if you don't, let your hands lie open.
A hymn in Gujri. Guru Arjan's crane, flying far while her chicks are cared for, and Bhagat Trilochan asking what fills the mind at the end. Today's word.
Your line: devotion in gujri. One voice soothes the anxious mind, and one wakes the distracted one. That's today, done.

howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Gujri hymn about the anxious mind and the crane is part of the Rehras, the evening prayer Sikhs recite or sing at sunset; in kirtan it is sung in Raga Gujri.

chat.says: Is that crane hymn telling people not to bother working or planning?
options: No. Sikh teaching prizes honest work; it eases the anxious mind that thinks all rests on it.
Yes. It says to stop working and simply wait, since God will provide everything.
No. It's only about birds, praising how well cranes raise their young.
